Red-eye round herring (Etrumeus acuminatus) is a pelagic clupeiform that exhibits clearly defined life-history milestones during its early development. At a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], freshly spawned eggs complete embryonic development and the yolk-sac larva emerges after approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days], a duration that aligns closely with incubation periods documented for other tropical clupeids. The newly hatched larva is entirely lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves until the mouth gapes and first exogenous feeding commences. The wet weight at this point of emergence, derived from measured egg diameters ranging between 1.3 and 1.47 millimeters, is estimated at 1.4e-3 grams [Wwb = 1.4e-3 grams], placing this species among the smaller propagules within the Dussumieriinae subfamily. This modest birth mass imposes a brief window during which successful first feeding must occur, or the larva risks reaching the point of no return. The incubation temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] also modulates the rate of yolk absorption, with lower temperatures prolonging the lecithotrophic phase and higher temperatures accelerating it, though consistent thermal conditions are maintained in these observations. Consequently, the early life stage remains tightly coupled to thermal conditions, a constraint that influences subsequent growth trajectories and the timing of the transition to the planktonic larval phase.

As larvae progress through the pelagic stage, somatic growth proceeds rapidly, driven by high feeding rates on copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton. Researchers have estimated the ultimate standard length that a fully grown adult can attain at 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a value consistent with the maximum sizes reported in taxonomic reviews of the genus Etrumeus from the Indo-West Pacific region and providing a benchmark against which the onset of reproductive maturation can be evaluated. Individuals typically reach puberty, defined by the initiation of gonadal development, at a standard length of 18.5 centimeters [Lp = 18.5 centimeters], indicating that approximately sixty percent of maximum somatic growth must be completed before reproductive physiology is activated. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from length–weight regressions specific to the species, is approximately 115 grams [Wwp = approximately 115 grams], reflecting the substantial mass gain required before resources are channeled toward gametogenesis. This size threshold is ecologically meaningful, as smaller individuals would likely face reduced fecundity or lower offspring viability if they attempted spawning prematurely. Field surveys consistently indicate that the transition from the juvenile to the maturing sub-adult stage is closely associated with this length milestone, after which growth continues but at a decelerated rate as reproductive investment increases.

Throughout the adult phase, the species exhibits iteroparous spawning behavior, with gravid individuals migrating to coastal aggregation sites to release pelagic eggs in multiple batches across a protracted breeding season. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum recorded body mass for a fully grown adult, has been calculated at 489 grams [Wwi = 489 grams] based on length–weight relationships extrapolated from a 30-centimeter standard length. This substantial mass supports the energetic demands of repeated spawning events, during which females may release several thousand eggs per spawning bout. Under the same thermal regime of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been measured at approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%]. This allocation strategy likely reflects a trade-off between current reproductive output and the preservation of somatic condition for future breeding seasons, a common pattern among iteroparous, medium-sized pelagic fish.

Longevity estimates indicate that Red-eye round herring exhibit a life span that is modest relative to many other teleosts. At the consistent temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum documented longevity reaches 6 years [am = 6 years], a value that emerges from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age validation in wild populations. This relatively short life span, combined with the early onset of reproduction at a standard length of 18.5 centimeters [Lp = 18.5 centimeters], implies that the species follows a comparatively fast life-history strategy, with most individuals contributing to only a few breeding seasons before senescence reduces condition and increases susceptibility to predation. Comparative analyses across the genus Etrumeus reveal that Red-eye round herring occupies an intermediate position in terms of body size and reproductive timing. The wet weight at puberty of 115 grams [Wwp = 115 grams] represents approximately 23.5 percent of the ultimate wet weight of 489 grams [Wwi = 489 grams], a proportion that aligns with the general clupeid pattern in which maturation occurs when roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of asymptotic mass has been accumulated. This relationship suggests that resources are directed toward growth until a sufficiently large body size is achieved, after which the balance shifts to include gamete production. The standard length at puberty of 18.5 centimeters [Lp = 18.5 centimeters] and the ultimate standard length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] together indicate that a length increase of only about sixty percent separates the onset of maturity from maximum size, a relatively compressed somatic growth window. The gonadosomatic index of approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] was observed in spawning females at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Overall, the life-history parameters of Etrumeus acuminatus reflect adaptation to a productive pelagic environment where high food availability supports rapid early growth, but where predation risk and thermal constraints impose limits on both size and longevity.
